title: Release data
text:
Portable export
Programmatically, a complete project can be exported with:
export_dir <- export_protvis_dataset(
  dataset,
  directory = "ProtVis_release",
  include_raw = FALSE
)
The export contains ProtVis_dataset.rds, expression/sample/protein tables, annotation files, process history, stored analysis results, metadata JSON, and an HTML report. Set include_raw = TRUE when attached input files should also be copied and licensing/privacy rules permit it.

title: Release data
text:
Manuscript-ready package
For a publication, keep a simple hierarchy such as:
ProtVis_release/
  data/
  metadata/
  statistics/
  enrichment/
  figures/
  methods/
  ProtVis_dataset.rds
Do not use screenshots as the only copy of a quantitative result. Export the table behind every key figure.






Tip



Record the ProtVis package version and the date of the final analysis. For actively developed software, a commit SHA or tagged release improves reproducibility further.

title: Data input

Raw/mzML
For Raw data, do not upload an artificial protein matrix simply to satisfy Project init. Register sample information, the mzML directory and FASTA; Project init creates a Sage_staging object. The conditional Search tab then runs Sage and creates the quantitative LFQ matrix.
Read Raw/mzML + Sage search for the complete workflow.

title: Data input

MaxQuant
When MaxQuant is selected, the source-specific MaxQuant Output Preparation item appears under Pre-processing. This is where MaxQuant-only unreliable evidence handling belongs. After that step, the dataset enters the same Correct Noise → Transformation → Imputation → Normalization sequence used by other sources.

Other tabular sources

Built-in compact examples are available for several input ecosystems and are useful for verifying that a parser and package installation are operational.
A programmatic example is:
library(ProtVis)

example_data <- load_protvis_builtin_data(
  source = "DIA-NN",
  auto_export = FALSE

example_data

title: Boxplot
text:
Workflow

Upload the Excel file.
Select the groups to display.
Choose pairwise comparisons.
Set x- and y-axis labels.
Customize group colors, box width, point size and outline color.
Choose a ggplot theme.
Review the statistical annotations.
Set output width/height and download the figure as PDF.

The current boxplot workflow uses pairwise t-tests via ggpubr::stat_compare_means.






Important



A t-test assumes an appropriate design and distributional model. Do not apply independent pairwise t-tests to paired/repeated-measures data without accounting for pairing, and consider multiple-testing correction when many comparisons are shown.

title: Protein structure
text:
Recommended workflow

Resolve the candidate to a stable protein identifier.
Obtain or upload the structure format expected by the selected toolkit.
Confirm chain/residue numbering before mapping a mutation, PTM or domain of interest.
Generate the interactive or static structural view.
Record the structure source and model/entry identifier in the figure legend or Methods.







Warning



Predicted structures and experimental structures are not equivalent evidence. When using a model, report its source and confidence/quality metrics and avoid over-interpreting poorly supported regions.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Use Toolkits → Correlation chord to explore relationships among numeric traits, proteins, metabolites, pathways or other quantitative variables. ProtVis calculates a correlation matrix from selected columns, filters relationships by absolute correlation, retains the strongest links up to a user-defined maximum, and displays the result as a chord diagram.
This module is designed for a focused correlation network rather than for drawing every possible pair. Filtering keeps the diagram interpretable and makes the exact displayed relationships available as a table.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Correlation Chord interface
The screenshot below shows the built-in example containing eight variables: Root_length, Shoot_length, Fresh_weight, Dry_weight, Proline, Sodium, Potassium, and Chlorophyll. In this example the analysis uses Pearson correlation and an absolute correlation threshold of 0.6; the displayed link counts belong only to this demonstration dataset.






Figure 1: ProtVis Correlation Chord interface showing example phenotype variables, correlation matrix, selected links, analysis summary and chord diagram.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load a numeric dataset. Under Input Data, upload .csv, .tsv, or .txt, or click Use Example Data. The built-in example contains 48 observations for the eight variables shown in the screenshot.
2. Select the variables. Use Select Numeric Columns to choose at least two numeric columns. ProtVis automatically offers only numeric variables from the loaded table.
3. Choose the correlation method. Under Analysis Settings, select pearson, spearman, or kendall. Pearson is the current default. Pearson summarizes linear association, whereas rank-based Spearman or Kendall can be more appropriate for monotonic relationships or data that do not satisfy Pearson assumptions.
4. Set the Absolute Correlation Threshold. The default is 0.6. ProtVis retains a pair only when abs(correlation) >= threshold, so the same cutoff applies to positive and negative relationships.
5. Set Maximum Number of Links. The current control ranges from 10 to 200 and defaults to 50. After the threshold filter, ProtVis sorts relationships by absolute correlation from strongest to weakest and keeps at most this many links. This limit is especially important when many variables are selected.
6. Click Run. ProtVis calculates the correlation matrix using pairwise-complete observations, removes self-correlations, collapses the two directions of each variable pair into one link, applies the absolute-correlation threshold, and then applies the maximum-link limit.
7. Review the previews before interpreting the diagram. Uploaded Data Preview shows the source values, Correlation Matrix Preview shows the complete selected-variable matrix, and Selected Links Preview shows the exact filtered edges that are sent to the chord diagram.
8. Check Analysis Summary. The summary reports status, number of selected variables, total links shown, positive and negative link counts, threshold, and correlation method. This provides a compact record of the settings behind the displayed network.
9. Adjust Display Settings. Label Size changes variable-label size; Link Transparency controls visual opacity; Positive Correlation Color and Negative Correlation Color set the two link classes. The current defaults are red #D73027 for positive and blue #4575B4 for negative correlations.
10. Export the result. The Download section provides PDF and PNG versions of the chord diagram plus correlation_matrix.csv. Keep the matrix together with the figure so the exact numerical relationships remain available independently of the visualization.

title: Correlation chord
text:
Input format
A typical input table has observations in rows and numeric variables in columns:
Root_length,Shoot_length,Fresh_weight,Proline,Sodium
12.3,18.4,5.8,1.21,0.42
10.9,16.7,5.1,1.56,0.71
14.2,20.1,6.3,0.98,0.35
Non-numeric columns can remain in the uploaded file, but only numeric columns are available for correlation analysis.

title: Correlation chord
text:
How links are selected
For the selected variables, ProtVis calls the correlation calculation with use = "pairwise.complete.obs". It then removes diagonal correlations and duplicate mirrored pairs such as A–B versus B–A. Pairs failing the absolute threshold are removed. The surviving pairs are ordered by |r| or the corresponding absolute rank-correlation coefficient, and only the strongest Maximum Number of Links are retained.
This means the chord diagram can intentionally show fewer relationships than the full correlation matrix. Use Selected Links Preview when you need the precise edge list represented in the figure.






WarningCorrelation is not causation



A strong chord indicates statistical association, not a causal relationship. For large correlation screens, also consider sample size, multiple testing, repeated-measures structure, and confounding variables before making biological conclusions.








Tip



If the diagram is crowded, increase the absolute-correlation threshold or reduce the maximum number of links rather than shrinking labels until the network becomes unreadable.

title: Toolkits

title: Toolkits
text:
How to use toolkits responsibly

Keep the input table used by the toolkit together with the exported figure.
Use stable protein/gene identifiers when moving between ProtVis and external databases.
Record species/taxonomy settings for database-backed tools.
Treat structure and network visualizations as evidence-supporting views, not automatic proof of mechanism.
Prefer the main workflow’s ProtVis_dataset results as the source of quantitative values rather than manually retyping numbers.

The sidebar provides dedicated pages for the most commonly used utilities.

title: Background make
text:
Background Maker interface
The screenshot below shows a completed maize example using annotations2.xlsx. The three summary cards report file status, GO annotation statistics and KEGG annotation statistics, while the two large tables preview the generated GO Background and KEGG Background records.






Figure 1: ProtVis Background Maker interface after processing an EggNOG annotation workbook. The sidebar contains file upload, gene-ID separator and action controls; the main panel reports file, GO and KEGG summaries and previews the generated background tables.



The values visible in this screenshot—such as 232,004 GO records and 13,763 KEGG records—belong only to this example annotation file and are not fixed ProtVis outputs.

title: Background make
text:
Required input
Upload an eggNOG output table in .csv, .xlsx, or .xls format. The current module requires these exact columns:
query
GOs
KEGG_Pathway
GOs and KEGG_Pathway may contain multiple comma-separated annotations for one query sequence.

title: Background make
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Upload the eggNOG annotation file. In File Upload, choose the annotation table. After upload, the file information panel shows the selected filename and the current validation state.
2. Check the file before generating a background. Click Check File. ProtVis verifies that query, GOs, and KEGG_Pathway are present. Continue only when the status reports File format check passed. The Run Background Maker action is intended to be used after this validation step.
3. Set the Gene ID Separator. The default separator is _. ProtVis uses this character to extract the stable ID from the beginning of the query field. For example:
Zm00001eb321680_T001
with _ becomes:
Zm00001eb321680
Choose a separator that matches the identifier convention of the uploaded annotation. Do not use _ automatically when your IDs follow a different scheme.
4. Run Background Maker. Click Run Background Maker. ProtVis expands comma-separated GO terms, retrieves GO term names from GO.db, removes unresolved GO annotations, and creates distinct GENE, TERM, NAME records. For KEGG, it keeps pathway IDs matching the map##### form and obtains pathway names from the KEGG pathway list when available.
5. Review the summary cards. FILE STATUS confirms whether the source file passed validation. GO SUMMARY and KEGG SUMMARY report record counts, unique genes and unique terms. Large differences between the number of source genes and annotated genes are expected when some genes lack GO or KEGG assignments, but unexpected losses should be investigated.
6. Inspect both output tables. The GO Background and KEGG Background cards show the enrichment-ready records. Each table should contain:
GENE
TERM
NAME
Check a few known genes and pathways before using the workbook for enrichment analysis.
7. Download the background workbook. Click Download Background. ProtVis writes a file named like background_YYYY-MM-DD.xlsx containing three worksheets: Summary, GO_background, and KEGG_background. The Summary sheet records the uploaded file and the generated record/gene/term counts.
8. Use Example Data when learning the format. Example Data downloads background_maker_example_data.csv, which can be used as a minimal template for the three required source columns.

title: Background make
section: How GO and KEGG records are generated
text:
How GO and KEGG records are generated
For GO annotations, ProtVis separates the comma-delimited GOs field, removes missing or - entries, extracts the stable gene ID, maps each GO ID to its term name, removes terms that cannot be resolved, and de-duplicates the resulting records.
For KEGG, ProtVis separates KEGG_Pathway, keeps valid map pathway identifiers such as map01100, and resolves pathway names through the KEGG pathway-list service. If a pathway-name lookup is unavailable, the current implementation can retain the pathway ID itself as the name rather than discarding that valid mapping.






ImportantUse the correct enrichment universe



The background should represent the genes/proteins that could realistically have been detected or tested in the experiment. Do not build the background only from significant proteins; doing so changes the statistical universe and can distort enrichment results.








Tip



Keep the generated workbook together with the eggNOG source file and record the annotation/database version. This makes later enrichment results substantially easier to reproduce.

title: Data transformation
text:
GUI workflow
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the transformation page after the six-sample PXD065315 example has been loaded and transformed with log10.






Figure 1: Data Transformation in ProtVis. The left panel is used to load the corrected matrix, choose a transformation method, and run the transformation. The upper cards display the original protein table and sample boxplot; the lower cards display the transformed table and transformed boxplot. The screenshot uses log10 as an example.



Follow the interface in this order. 1. Load data. Click Load data. ProtVis uses the active ProtVis_dataset first and can recover Step3_correct_noise.rda for legacy projects. Confirm that the load status changes to Data loaded and that the upper Original Data table contains the expected protein IDs and sample columns.
2. Choose the Transformation Method. Select the intended method in the sidebar. The screenshot uses log10 only as a worked example; it is not a universal recommendation. Check the original boxplot before transforming so you know whether the values are strongly right-skewed, already logarithmic, standardized, or centered.
3. Run the transformation. Click Run transformation. After completion, the status panel reports the current method and the lower Transformed Data table and visualization are refreshed. Compare the upper and lower panels rather than judging only from the numeric table: the transformed distributions should reflect the mathematical operation you selected without changing sample identity or protein order unexpectedly.
The color selectors and plot width/height controls affect presentation and downloaded plots only; they do not alter the quantitative matrix. Download the original and transformed PDF plots when they are part of the analysis record.

title: Data transformation
text:
Interpreting the worked log10 example
Current ProtVis applies log10(x + 1e-8) for the log10 option and log2(x + 1e-8) for log2. Consequently, an exact zero can appear close to -8.00 after log10, as visible in the screenshot. In the following imputation stage, ProtVis treats legacy not-observed sentinels such as 0 and -8 as missing rather than as biological abundance.
For many positive intensity-based proteomics datasets, a logarithmic transform can reduce right-skew and compress large abundance differences. Standardization or Z-score transformations are more appropriate for some pattern-oriented analyses but change the interpretation of absolute values. The intended downstream model should therefore guide the choice.






WarningCheck the input scale first



Do not apply an additional log transformation to data that are already logarithmic. Also inspect zero and missing-value behavior before moving to imputation; a displayed -8 in the current log10 workflow can represent a transformed zero rather than a genuine measured abundance.

title: Data transformation
text:
Output
The transformed state is written to the active ProtVis_dataset, recorded in process history with the selected method, and persisted in the compatibility file:
Step4_data_transformed.rda
Continue with Data imputation.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
Once an input route has produced a real protein-by-sample matrix, ProtVis uses four source-independent preprocessing modules:
Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization
Keeping these decisions separate makes it easier to inspect the effect of each operation and to record the selected method in project history.
For Raw/mzML, run Search first. A Sage_staging object deliberately has no expression matrix and cannot enter Correct Noise until Sage LFQ has been finalized.
For MaxQuant, complete the conditional MaxQuant Output Preparation step first. Other supported tabular sources enter preprocessing after their source-specific parser/import has produced the canonical matrix.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
1. Correct noise
Correct Noise is the first shared preprocessing stage. It prefers the active ProtVis_dataset; if recovery from disk is needed, Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda is the canonical cross-source handoff. Raw/Sage also retains Step2_sage_database_search.rda as a compatibility snapshot.
The correction itself is replicate-aware. For sample groups whose names contain replicate suffixes such as _1, _2, and _3, zero/missing cells are corrected only when sufficient non-zero replicate evidence exists; otherwise the affected replicate group remains missing. Duplicate protein IDs are collapsed safely before reshaping.
Read Correct noise.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
2. Data transformation
ProtVis currently exposes None, log10, log2, Standardization, Z-Score, scale, center, and scale-center. Original and transformed distributions can be compared before proceeding.
Read Data transformation.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
3. Data imputation
Missing measurements are visualized before imputation. The current GUI offers kNN, RF, Mean, Median, Zero, and Minimum, with kNN selected by default. Legacy missing sentinels such as 0 and -8 are kept as true NA until the user runs imputation.
Read Data imputation.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
4. Data normalization
The current normalization module performs column-wise median subtraction, centering each sample by its median. Original and normalized boxplots can be compared and downloaded.
Read Data normalization.

title: Pre-processing workflow
text:
Duplicate-run protection
Current ProtVis protects important run buttons at two levels: the interface disables an active run button while Shiny is busy, and server-side guards reject the same operation if it is already executing. This is particularly important for Sage search and preprocessing steps, where an accidental double click could otherwise create duplicate work or competing output files.






WarningDo not impute before inspecting missingness



Missing values in proteomics are not always random. Use the missing-value visualization and the biological design to decide whether a global imputation strategy is appropriate for your experiment.

title: Pre-processing workflow
section: What to check before downstream analysis
text:
What to check before downstream analysis
Before opening Overview or DEP analysis, verify that sample names match sample_info, no sample is unexpectedly all missing, transformed values are on the intended scale, imputation did not create implausible distributions, and normalization reduced unwanted sample-level shifts without erasing known biological differences.

title: Data normalization
text:
The current ProtVis normalization module performs median subtraction. For each numeric sample column, ProtVis subtracts that column’s median (ignoring NA values):
\[x'_{ij} = x_{ij} - \operatorname{median}(x_{\cdot j})\]
After normalization, each sample is centered around a comparable median while relative within-sample differences are retained.

title: Data normalization
text:
GUI workflow
The screenshot below shows the normalization page after the six-sample example has passed transformation and imputation.






Figure 1: Data Normalization in ProtVis. The numbered controls show the recommended order: 1 load the imputed data and 2 run median-subtraction normalization. The upper panels show original values and their boxplot; the lower panels show normalized values and the normalized boxplot.



Follow the two numbered controls. 1. Load data. Click Load data. The module uses the current imputed ProtVis_dataset first and can recover Step5_data_imputation.rda for compatibility. Confirm that the interface reports Data loaded, then inspect the upper Original Data table and boxplot. Sample columns should still match the project sample information.
2. Run normalization. Click Run normalization. ProtVis subtracts each sample column’s median and reports Median subtraction normalization completed when the operation succeeds. Inspect the lower Normalized Data table and visualization immediately after completion.
Compare the upper and lower boxplots rather than relying on the status message alone. Median subtraction should center broad sample-level offsets while preserving within-sample rank differences. The plot-color controls and download dimensions are presentation settings only; they do not change the stored normalized matrix.

title: Data normalization
text:
Interpretation
Median subtraction is useful when broad sample-level offsets are considered technical rather than biological. It is not appropriate to assume this for every experimental design. If most proteins are expected to shift globally in one biological direction, inspect the distributions carefully before interpreting normalized fold changes.






TipCheck the full preprocessing sequence



The screenshot belongs at the end of the shared preprocessing route: Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization. Before moving to differential abundance analysis, confirm that sample names are unchanged, imputation did not create implausible distributions, and normalization improved technical comparability without erasing the expected group pattern.

title: Data normalization
text:
Output
The normalized project state is written to the active ProtVis_dataset and persisted as:
Step6_data_normalization.rda
This stage is the standard input for Overview and DEP analysis.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
The standard downstream workflow begins after Data Normalization. ProtVis then provides two complementary views of the data:

Overview asks whether the dataset is technically and biologically coherent.
DEP analysis asks which proteins differ between defined groups.

Functional modules such as enrichment, GSEA, Pathview and PPI should be interpreted in the context of those upstream checks.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Recommended order

Overview & QC — inspect correlations, distributions, missingness, PCA/CV and dimensionality-reduction structure.
DEP analysis — run one or more explicit Group1 versus Group2 comparisons.
Enrichment analysis — test significant protein IDs against GO/KEGG backgrounds.
GSEA — use a ranked signal when a thresholded DEP list would discard useful pathway-level information.
Pathview — project KO-level log fold changes onto a selected KEGG pathway.
Add STRINGdb PPI, WGCNA, co-enrichment or other network/integration modules when relevant.







ImportantSeparate statistical evidence from visualization settings



Changing colors, point sizes, heatmap labels or plot dimensions should not change the underlying statistical model. In contrast, changing a fold-change or p-value threshold changes which proteins are labeled significant and therefore affects heatmaps and downstream gene lists.

title: Downstream analysis
text:
Canonical data flow
Current modules prefer the active ProtVis_dataset. Compatibility stage files remain readable when a project is reopened. Downstream results are stored in analysis_results and process history so the quantitative matrix and derived statistics stay connected.

title: Enrichment analysis
text:
Enrichment analysis uses two components:

a gene/protein ID list;
an Enrichment Analysis File containing the GO and KEGG background definitions.



The current module follows this priority:

an uploaded gene-list file (.csv or .xlsx);
IDs pasted in manual mode;
significant IDs from the selected DEP comparison.

Uploaded/pasted gene-list data should contain an ID column. The parser also recognizes common variants such as gene/protein ID names, but using ID is the most portable choice.



Upload one .xlsx workbook with both worksheets:
GO_background
KEGG_background
Each worksheet must contain:
TERM   GENE   NAME
TERM is the ontology/pathway identifier, GENE contains associated IDs (multiple IDs can be separated by common delimiters), and NAME is the human-readable term name.
After clicking Check File, ProtVis previews the first rows of both sheets. A validated workbook is stored with the active ProtVis_dataset; when it is selected before Project init, ProtVis retains it and attaches it when the project object is created.

title: Overview

ProtVis interface






Figure 1: ProtVis Homepage after launch. The top navigation provides direct access to Project init, Search, Pre-processing, Downstream analysis, Multi-omics, PTM, Release data, Toolkits, and Help. The Homepage summarizes the central ProtVis_dataset architecture and the major workflow components.

title: Overview
text:
Source-aware navigation
The selected source controls only the route-specific entry step; shared preprocessing remains available afterward.

Raw shows the top-level Search tab and uses Sage to create the protein LFQ matrix.
MaxQuant shows Pre-processing → MaxQuant Output Preparation.
Other tabular sources use their parser/import route and then enter shared preprocessing.

This keeps MaxQuant-only filtering out of Raw, DIA-NN, Spectronaut and other workflows while still converging on the same ProtVis_dataset model.

title: Overview
text:
The key architecture: ProtVis_dataset
Earlier ProtVis workflows were described primarily as a chain of .rda files. Current ProtVis keeps those stage files for compatibility and recovery, but the canonical representation is now a validated ProtVis_dataset object.
A project object keeps the protein-by-sample expression matrix aligned with sample and protein metadata, stores fixed annotation layers (eggnog_output, GO_annotation, and KEGG_annotation), records analysis/search results, and captures process history and checkpoint information. See ProtVis_dataset for the full model.
Raw/Sage adds one deliberate staging state: Project init may create a Sage_staging object before the expression matrix exists. After Sage LFQ completes, the same project is finalized into the normal protein-by-sample structure.






ImportantWhy this matters



A result should not be separated from the data and parameters that produced it. ProtVis therefore creates traceable object states as analysis proceeds instead of treating each plot or search output as an isolated end product.

title: Overview
text:
Recommended routes
For Raw/mzML:
Project init → Search → Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization → Overview → DEP analysis → Enrichment/GSEA/Pathview
For MaxQuant:
Project init → MaxQuant Output Preparation → Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization → Overview → DEP analysis → Enrichment/GSEA/Pathview
For the other supported quantitative tables, use the corresponding parser/import path and then join the shared preprocessing sequence at Correct Noise.
Then add WGCNA, PPI, co-enrichment, metaproteomics, PTM, or other specialized modules when they address the biological question.

The GUI is intended for interactive exploration, parameter selection, and figure export. Reproducibility is supported by the persisted ProtVis_dataset, stage snapshots, process history, checkpoints, portable exports, Sage configuration/result retention, and duplicate-run guards for important execution buttons.

title: Venn
text:
Venn / UpSet interface
The screenshot below shows the current module with the built-in three-set demonstration data. The example contains Proteome, Transcriptome, and Phosphoproteome sets and is currently displayed in Venn mode. The right side contains the intersection plot and the processed binary membership table.






Figure 1: ProtVis Venn/UpSet module using the built-in Proteome, Transcriptome and Phosphoproteome example. The sidebar provides file input, example data, plot-type selection and per-set colors, while the main panel displays the overlap plot and processed membership table.

title: Venn
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Prepare a set-membership CSV. Each column represents one set and each non-empty cell contains a feature identifier. The sets do not need to have the same number of members; shorter columns can contain empty/NA cells.
2. Load the data. Use File to upload a .csv, or click Use example data. The built-in example contains three sets named Proteome, Transcriptome and Phosphoproteome and is displayed immediately after loading.
3. Confirm the detected set count. The status message above the plot reports the number of sets and the current rendering mode, for example Detected 3 sets. Current mode: VENN.
4. Choose the plot type. Under Choose plot type, select Auto, Venn, or UpSet. Auto uses Venn for up to six sets and UpSet for more than six. If Venn is forced for more than six sets, ProtVis warns you to use Auto or UpSet instead.
5. Set colors. After loading data, ProtVis creates one color selector for each set. In the example these are Select Color for Proteome, Select Color for Transcriptome, and Select Color for Phosphoproteome. Color settings affect the Venn presentation; UpSet rendering follows the UpSet layout.
6. Run the plot when using uploaded data or after changing settings. Click Run to rebuild the current Venn/UpSet result from the selected plot mode and colors. The built-in example is initialized immediately, but rerunning is appropriate after changing display settings.
7. Inspect the overlap plot. For a small number of sets, Venn provides a direct visual summary of unique and shared members. For larger comparisons, UpSet is easier to read because intersections are represented as a matrix of active sets with frequency bars rather than increasingly complex overlapping circles.
8. Inspect the Processed Table. ProtVis converts the source sets to a binary membership table in which each unique feature occupies one row and each set is encoded as 1 (present) or 0 (absent). The table can be searched and exported with the built-in Copy, CSV, and Excel controls.
9. Export the figure. Click Download to save the current visualization as PDF. Venn exports use an 8 × 6 inch layout, while UpSet uses a 10 × 7 inch PDF canvas in the current implementation.

title: Venn
text:
Input format
A suitable CSV looks like this:
Proteome,Transcriptome,Phosphoproteome
P53,P53,AKT1
MAPK1,MAPK1,MTOR
AKT1,HIF1A,MAPK1
MTOR,STAT3,EGFR
STAT3,JUN,SRC
EGFR,,JUN
ProtVis trims surrounding whitespace, treats blank cells as missing, and removes duplicate identifiers within each set before constructing the overlap representation.

title: Venn
text:
Venn versus UpSet
A Venn diagram is most useful for a small number of sets because the individual intersections remain visually interpretable. UpSet is preferable when the number of sets becomes larger or when many different intersections must be compared quantitatively.
The Auto option is therefore the recommended default for general use: it preserves the intuitive Venn view for small comparisons while avoiding unreadable diagrams for larger set collections.

title: Venn
text:
Interpretation
Overlap size is descriptive: it tells you which identifiers are shared between sets, not whether the overlap is statistically greater than expected by chance. A formal overlap-enrichment test requires a clearly defined background universe and an appropriate statistical model.
Also confirm that all columns use the same identifier namespace before interpretation. Apparent non-overlap can simply reflect incompatible gene/protein ID systems.






Tip



Use the Processed Table when you need exact membership for downstream analysis. The figure is ideal for communication, but the binary table is the reproducible record of which features belong to each intersection.








Note



The P53/MAPK1/AKT1-style identifiers shown in the screenshot belong to ProtVis’s built-in demonstration dataset and are intended only to illustrate input structure and plotting behavior.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Use Multi-omics → Nine quadrant to compare two quantitative effect estimates, most commonly matched log2FC values from two omics layers or two related contrasts. ProtVis divides the x- and y-axes with the same absolute fold-change cutoff and assigns every row to one of nine directional classes: Up/Up, Up/NS, Up/Down, NS/Up, NS/NS, NS/Down, Down/Up, Down/NS, and Down/Down.
This view is useful for separating concordant changes, discordant changes, and changes detected mainly in one omics layer.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Nine-quadrant interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current module with the bundled demonstration data. The built-in example contains 2,800 rows × 4 columns: Omic1_ID, Log2FC_Omic1, Omic2_ID, and Log2FC_Omic2. The quadrant counts visible in this run are example-specific and will change with another dataset or cutoff.






Figure 1: ProtVis Nine-quadrant interface using the built-in two-omics demonstration dataset. The left sidebar contains Data Input, Plot Settings, Color Settings and Download Settings. The center card previews the input table and the right card displays the nine-quadrant plot and quadrant-specific result panels.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Load the data. Open Data Input and either upload a .csv/.xlsx file or click LOAD DEMO DATA. The demonstration dataset is not loaded automatically. Use Download example CSV when you want a template for preparing your own file.
2. Check the preview. The Uploaded Data Preview card should show the expected row and column counts. ProtVis requires at least two numeric columns for the plot.
3. Select the x- and y-axis variables. Choose the numeric field for Select Omic1 (X-axis) and the numeric field for Select Omic2 (Y-axis). In the built-in example these are Log2FC_Omic1 and Log2FC_Omic2.
4. Set the fold-change cutoff. Open Plot Settings and set Log2FC Cutoff. The current default is 1. ProtVis uses +cutoff and -cutoff on both axes: values above +cutoff are Up, values below -cutoff are Down, and values between the thresholds are NS.
5. Control quadrant labels. Keep Show Quadrant Counts selected if you want the number of rows in each of the nine regions to be displayed on the figure.
6. Run the plot. Click Run plot. The status badge changes to Ready when the classification and plot have been generated.
7. Inspect the biological direction classes. Up/Up and Down/Down represent concordant responses, whereas Up/Down and Down/Up represent opposite responses. Up/NS, Down/NS, NS/Up, and NS/Down indicate that only one selected layer crosses the fold-change threshold. NS/NS contains rows within the cutoff on both axes.
8. Inspect and export the quadrant tables. Below the plot, ProtVis creates expandable panels for all nine classes. Each panel contains the corresponding rows and provides an individual CSV download button, which is useful for taking a selected directional class into enrichment or network analysis.
9. Export the figure. Under Download Settings, set the PDF width and height and click Download PDF. The current defaults are 8 × 6 inches.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Input format
A minimal file can contain separate identifiers for the two layers and one numeric effect column for each layer:
Omic1_ID,Log2FC_Omic1,Omic2_ID,Log2FC_Omic2
Gene_001,1.52,Protein_001,1.18
Gene_002,-2.10,Protein_002,-1.43
Gene_003,0.35,Protein_003,1.76
The selected x- and y-axis columns must be numeric. Other columns can remain in the input and will be retained in the preview and exported quadrant tables.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Color settings
Open Color Settings to customize all nine classes independently: Up_Up, Down_Down, Up_Down, Down_Up, Up_NS, Down_NS, NS_Up, NS_Down, and NS_NS. Color changes affect presentation only; they do not change class membership.

title: Nine quadrant
text:
Interpretation
The nine-quadrant module performs directional classification from the selected numeric values and cutoff. It is not a substitute for formal differential statistics. When available, perform the appropriate DEP/DEG analysis first and retain adjusted p-values or significance labels alongside the fold changes.






WarningKeep contrast direction consistent



If one layer uses Treatment - Control while the other uses Control - Treatment, biologically concordant responses will appear discordant. Verify contrast direction before interpreting the quadrant pattern.








Note



The built-in 2,800-row dataset is a demonstration dataset intended to show the interface and output structure. The quadrant counts in the screenshot are not expected values for real experiments.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
The current WGCNA module provides a complete sequence from data filtering to network interpretation:
Data cleaning → Filtering → Soft threshold → Module detection → Trait association → Interested module → Hub gene/protein → Cytoscape export
Although some UI labels use “gene”, the module can analyze protein abundance matrices.

title: WGCNA
text:
Input
Upload a .txt, .tsv, or .csv expression matrix. The first column should contain feature IDs and the remaining columns should be samples. The format selector includes count, expected count, normalized count, peak area (metabolomics), and protein abundance.
Select an unsigned or signed network and the appropriate preprocessing/normalization mode for the supplied data.

title: WGCNA
text:
Filtering
The first filter removes low-abundance features based on sample percentage and expression cutoff. The second filter ranks variability using MAD or Variance and retains the requested number of features.
Filtering is especially important for proteomics because a network built from thousands of uninformative or extremely sparse proteins can be unstable and computationally expensive.

title: WGCNA
text:
Soft-threshold selection
Run the soft-threshold analysis, review the scale-free topology fit, and either use the recommended power or specify a justified custom power. The default target displayed by the UI is an \(R^2\) cutoff of 0.8.

title: WGCNA
text:
Module detection
Set minimum module size, module merge/cut-tree height, and maximum block size, then run module detection. Export the protein-to-module table so every downstream claim can be traced back to module membership.

title: WGCNA
text:
Trait association
Upload trait data and run module-trait analysis. Check sample names carefully: trait rows/columns must correspond to the same samples represented in the expression matrix.

title: WGCNA
text:
Hub proteins and Cytoscape
Select a trait and module, set absolute kME/GS cutoffs, and run hub analysis. ProtVis can generate node and edge tables for Cytoscape using a user-defined network-weight threshold.






Warning



WGCNA requires enough samples to estimate correlations meaningfully. Very small proteomics experiments can produce visually convincing but unstable networks. Treat network topology cautiously when sample size is limited.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
ProtVis_dataset is an independent S4 class designed for proteomics. It does not inherit from mass_dataset and does not require the massdataset package. Its validity checks enforce exact alignment between expression columns and sample_info, and between expression rows and variable_info.
This architecture allows ProtVis to preserve one coherent scientific record while every module adds a new result or processing step.






Figure 1: Conceptual architecture of ProtVis_dataset. Expression data are linked to sample and variable metadata, annotation resources, analysis results, processing history, and provenance/extra files to support interoperability, reproducibility, and recoverability.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Create a dataset programmatically
library(ProtVis)

expr <- data.frame(
  S1 = c(10, 20, 30),
  S2 = c(12, 18, 33),
  row.names = c("P1", "P2", "P3")
)

samples <- data.frame(
  sample_id = c("S1", "S2"),
  group = c("Control", "Treatment"),
  row.names = c("S1", "S2")
)

ds <- create_protvis_dataset(
  expression_data = expr,
  sample_info = samples,
  metadata = list(source = "User-defined matrix")
)

validate_protvis_dataset(ds)
For day-to-day GUI use, Project init creates this object automatically.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Inspect a built-in project
library(ProtVis)

ds <- load_protvis_builtin_data(
  source = "DIA-NN",
  auto_export = FALSE
)

class(ds)
slotNames(ds)
dim(ds$expression_data)
head(ds$sample_info)
Use protvis_expression_matrix(ds) when you need an ID-first data frame suitable for UI boundaries or export.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
The Raw/Sage staging exception
A normal validated ProtVis_dataset must contain a non-empty numeric expression layer aligned to its sample and variable metadata. The current class has one deliberate exception: a project whose metadata marks workflow_stage = "Sage_staging" may temporarily have an empty expression layer.
This supports a scientifically correct Raw workflow:
sample metadata + FASTA + mzML registration → Sage search → protein LFQ matrix
Instead of inventing protein values before a search exists, Project init creates:
ProtVis_dataset__project_init__Sage_staging__v1
After Sage succeeds, the LFQ table is converted to the protein matrix and the object is finalized as a normal quantitative project, for example:
ProtVis_dataset__Sage_database_search__v2
The parent/staging information and process history remain available in the finalized object.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Sage results and provenance
A completed Sage search is stored under:
ds$analysis_results$Sage_database_search
The bundle includes search status, configuration, result-file paths, log information, PSM table and LFQ table. Search metadata also records the FASTA, mzML directory, output directory and Sage engine version.
Produced files that exist on disk are registered in other_files with filename, normalized path, file size, MD5 checksum and attachment timestamp. Raw mzML/FASTA bytes are not duplicated into the S4 object itself; the object records the analytical context and result provenance while the project directory retains the files.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Object versions
ProtVis analysis helpers create traceable object versions rather than overwriting an unnamed global object. Object names encode the project stage or method, and the object retains parameters and process history so results can be related back to their analytical context.
For long-running GUI actions, current ProtVis also protects against duplicate execution. This matters for object versioning because an accidental second click should not create an unintended parallel search or preprocessing state.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Annotation schema
The annotation slot always exposes the same three named data frames:
names(ds$annotation)
# eggnog_output, GO_annotation, KEGG_annotation
Missing annotation layers are represented as empty data frames rather than changing the object schema. This makes downstream code more predictable.

title: ProtVis_dataset
text:
Export a portable project
out <- export_protvis_dataset(
  ds,
  directory = "ProtVis_export",
  include_raw = FALSE
)

out
The export bundle contains the serialized ProtVis_dataset, expression and metadata tables, annotation tables, process history, serialized analysis results, a metadata JSON file, and an HTML report. If include_raw = TRUE, available attached source files can also be copied where supported.






ImportantTreat the object as the authoritative record



Stage .rda files are useful for compatibility and recovery, but new analyses should use the active ProtVis_dataset whenever possible. This prevents parameters, annotation, search provenance, and file context from becoming detached from the quantitative matrix.

ProtVis combines data import, Raw/mzML database search, preprocessing, quality control, statistical analysis, functional interpretation, multi-omics integration, PTM analysis, and publication-ready visualization in one interactive workflow. This cookbook follows the application in the same order that a real project is analyzed.
Start with installation · Run Raw/mzML + Sage · Understand ProtVis_dataset

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
ProtVis at a glance
The overview below shows how heterogeneous proteomics software outputs are brought into ProtVis_dataset, processed through a shared preprocessing and quality-control workflow, and connected to differential analysis, functional interpretation, multi-omics, WGCNA, and key-protein characterization.






Figure 1: Overview Workflow in ProtVis. Heterogeneous proteomics software outputs enter a unified ProtVis_dataset workflow spanning preprocessing, data summary, downstream analysis, multi-omics integration, WGCNA, and key-protein characterization.





Heterogeneous input

Import MaxQuant, Proteome Discoverer, DIA-NN, Spectronaut, FragPipe, Skyline, OpenMS, Mascot, or a user-defined matrix.



Raw/mzML + Sage

Register sample metadata, validate mzML filenames, upload a protein FASTA, run Sage, and convert LFQ results directly into the canonical project object.



Traceable data object

Carry expression data, sample and protein metadata, annotations, results, imported files, parameters, and process history in ProtVis_dataset.



Proteomics preprocessing

Correct replicate-level noise, transform intensities, inspect missingness, impute missing values, and normalize samples.



QC and statistics

Use correlation, expression-pattern heatmaps, PCA/PCoA/t-SNE/UMAP/NMDS, proteomics QC, and limma-based differential abundance analysis.



Biological interpretation

Continue from DEP results into GO/KEGG enrichment, GSEA, Pathview, STRINGdb PPI, WGCNA, and co-enrichment.



Beyond standard proteomics

Explore metaproteomics, expression profiles, nine-quadrant integration, Venn analysis, PTMs, strict spectra, and protein structure utilities.

title: ProtVis Cookbook
text:
Recommended analysis paths
For Raw/mzML data, use:
Project init → Search → Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization → Overview → DEP → Interpretation
For MaxQuant, use:
Project init → MaxQuant Output Preparation → Correct Noise → Data Transformation → Data Imputation → Data Normalization → Overview → DEP → Interpretation
For other supported tabular outputs, import/parse the source-specific quantitative table and continue into the shared preprocessing workflow.
The Raw route is intentionally different: Project init can create a sample-only Sage staging ProtVis_dataset without inventing an expression matrix. The protein-by-sample matrix is created after the Sage LFQ search succeeds.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
ProtVis defines an ordered analysis progression from creation/import through preprocessing, dimensionality reduction, differential analysis, enrichment, and network analysis. Checkpoints capture a validated ProtVis_dataset at a named stage.






Figure 1: Checkpoint-aware analysis and recovery in ProtVis. Auto-saved validated stages support resuming interrupted analyses or restarting downstream analysis from a selected stage, while the interface design isolates node-level failures and preserves available checkpoints.



The important principle is that the active ProtVis_dataset is authoritative. Checkpoints and stage .rda files make that object recoverable; they are not parallel, unrelated data models.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Save a checkpoint
checkpoint <- save_protvis_checkpoint(
  dataset = ds,
  directory = "checkpoints",
  stage = "normalization",
  keep = 20
)

checkpoint
Checkpoint files use names beginning with:
protvis_checkpoint_<stage>_...rds
Saving is validated before a checkpoint is published, reducing the chance that a partial write replaces a usable analysis state.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
List and restore checkpoints
list_protvis_checkpoints("checkpoints")
The returned table includes the file path, stage, creation time, size, MD5, and whether the checkpoint can be read.
Restore the newest checkpoint with:
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  version = "latest"
)
Or request a stage:
restored <- restore_protvis_checkpoint(
  "checkpoints",
  stage = "differential_analysis"
)
If the exact requested stage is unavailable, ProtVis can select the newest readable checkpoint at or before that stage.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Automatic persistence
Many GUI stages persist the active object automatically. protvis_auto_export_dataset() writes a portable export bundle and records the latest output location in the dataset metadata.
ds <- protvis_auto_export_dataset(
  ds,
  directory = getwd(),
  include_raw = FALSE
)
The GUI also protects long-running actions against duplicate execution. Buttons marked as run actions are disabled while Shiny is busy, and key server modules independently reject the same action if it is already running. This prevents accidental double searches, imports, or preprocessing runs from creating competing checkpoints.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Source-independent Step2
The current preprocessing handoff uses:
Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda
as the canonical Step2 file across data sources. The historical filename remains for compatibility, but the contents are a ProtVis_dataset and can originate from MaxQuant, Sage, or another supported input route.
For Raw/Sage, a successful search also writes:
Step2_sage_database_search.rda
The Sage-specific file is retained as a compatibility/recovery snapshot. Correct Noise prefers the active object and then the canonical Step2 file.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Sage search recovery
Raw/Sage projects have an additional recovery path. If the Shiny session restarts after Sage completed, ProtVis can reconstruct the search bundle from the existing Sage_search directory when the LFQ result and input context are still resolvable.
The expected Sage files are:
Sage_search/
├── sage_config.json
├── results.sage.tsv
├── lfq.tsv
└── results.json
lfq.tsv is required for recovery of the quantitative protein matrix. The stored configuration is used to recover FASTA and mzML context when possible.
This means a completed database search does not need to be rerun merely because the application session closed.

title: Checkpoints & recovery
text:
Compatibility stage files
Common stage files currently include:
Step1_project_init.rda
Step2_remove_unreliable_peptide.rda
Step2_sage_database_search.rda   # Raw/Sage compatibility snapshot
Step3_correct_noise.rda
Step4_data_transformed.rda
Step5_data_imputation.rda
Step6_data_normalization.rda
Step7_differential_analysis.rda
Current snapshots are written with exactly one ProtVis_dataset object. Older workspaces that stored expression and sample objects separately can still be migrated by the internal loading layer where supported.






TipRecovery strategy



Keep the complete working directory together with the latest portable export, checkpoint directory, and—when using Raw/Sage—the Sage_search directory. This preserves the serialized project, human-readable exports, search evidence, and stage-aware recovery options in one place.

title: Expression profile
text:
Use Multi-omics → Expression profile when the biological question concerns coordinated abundance trends across several samples, stages, tissues, genotypes or conditions rather than only one pairwise comparison. The current interface provides two complementary views: Kmeans trend clustering and a Heatmap trend-analysis mode.
The Kmeans workflow standardizes each feature across samples before clustering, so the resulting trajectories emphasize relative expression patterns rather than absolute protein abundance. Cluster membership can then be exported for downstream enrichment or network analyses.

title: Expression profile
text:
Expression profile interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current Kmeans interface using the bundled example data. The example contains 582 features × 8 samples and is clustered into six groups. The cluster sizes displayed in this particular run are Cluster1 = 64, Cluster2 = 169, Cluster3 = 115, Cluster4 = 105, Cluster5 = 56 and Cluster6 = 73; these counts are example-specific and will change with another matrix, sample order or number of centers.






Figure 1: ProtVis Expression profile Kmeans interface. The left panel provides CSV upload, Load built-in example, Download example CSV and method selection. The main Kmeans card contains Parameter, Run and Download controls plus Figure, Table and Input Data tabs. Six trend clusters are displayed for the built-in 582-feature by 8-sample example.

title: Expression profile
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Choose the input data. Upload an expression matrix as a .csv, or click Load built-in example to load the bundled kmeans.csv. The built-in file is not loaded automatically. After loading, confirm the green status message and inspect the Input Data tab before running clustering. The first column is used as the feature identifier and the remaining columns must be numeric sample values.
2. Download the example when preparing your own file. Click Download example CSV to obtain the same kmeans.csv used by ProtVis. This is the easiest way to confirm the required file structure before replacing the example values with your own protein-expression matrix.
3. Select the analysis method. Under Method, choose Kmeans for trend clusters or Heatmap for the heatmap-based trend view. The screenshot shows Kmeans selected.
4. Set the Kmeans parameters. Open Parameter. Choose the line color and set centers, which is the requested number of K-means clusters. The current default is 6. Use a biologically defensible value rather than increasing K only to make the figure appear more detailed.
5. Run Kmeans. Open Run and click Run. ProtVis standardizes each feature across the sample columns and then applies stats::kmeans() with the selected number of centers. The black line in each cluster panel represents the cluster-center trajectory, while the colored lines represent individual feature trajectories.
6. Review all three result tabs. Use Figure to inspect the trend panels, Table to review feature-to-cluster assignments, and Input Data to return to the matrix that generated the result. Check that the sample order on the x-axis follows the intended biological sequence; K-means does not infer chronological or treatment order for you.
7. Export the result. In Download, set the desired figure width and height, then download the Kmeans Figure as PDF and the cluster Table as CSV. Keep the cluster table when using cluster-specific protein sets for enrichment, annotation or network analysis.

title: Expression profile
text:
Input format
A suitable CSV has feature identifiers in the first column and numeric samples in the remaining columns, for example:
ID,Sample1,Sample2,Sample3,Sample4
Protein_A,10.2,12.4,18.7,21.1
Protein_B,30.5,24.2,17.9,11.6
Protein_C,8.1,14.6,13.9,20.4
ProtVis requires at least two sample columns, and all sample columns must be numeric. If samples represent an ordered experiment, arrange them in the intended chronological or biological order before clustering because that column order becomes the trend-plot x-axis.

title: Expression profile
text:
How Kmeans is calculated
For the Kmeans view, ProtVis scales each feature across samples before clustering. Conceptually, each row is transformed to a standardized trajectory and K-means then groups rows with similar shapes. This means a highly abundant protein and a low-abundance protein can enter the same cluster when their relative trajectories are similar.
The cluster title includes both the cluster number and the number of assigned features. In the bundled example shown above, six clusters contain a total of 582 features.






ImportantInterpret trend shape, not absolute abundance



Because Kmeans uses row-standardized values, the y-axis represents standardized relative change. Do not interpret the plotted y-value as the original protein intensity. Return to the original/normalized quantitative matrix when absolute abundance is required.

title: Expression profile
text:
Heatmap mode
Selecting Heatmap opens the Heatmap trend analysis (K-means) view. Set the number of K-means clusters and choose the scale mode: Row (trend), Column, or None. Run the heatmap and inspect the resulting cluster structure before exporting the cluster table.
Row scaling is appropriate when the goal is to emphasize within-protein trends across samples. Column scaling instead emphasizes sample-wise relative structure, while None retains the supplied numerical scale.

title: Expression profile
text:
Choosing the number of clusters
There is no universally correct K. Start with a moderate number, inspect cluster size and trajectory coherence, and compare nearby values when needed. Very large K values can fragment one coherent response into many small groups, whereas very small K values can merge distinct biological patterns.
A useful cluster should contain a recognizable trajectory and enough members to support the intended downstream interpretation. A cluster containing only a handful of proteins is not automatically wrong, but it deserves closer inspection before biological conclusions are drawn.

title: Expression profile
text:
Downstream use
Exported cluster assignments can be used to create cluster-specific protein lists for Enrichment analysis, pathway interpretation, PPI/network analysis, or other multi-omics modules. Preserve the sample order, preprocessing state, selected K and cluster table as part of the analysis record so that the trend analysis can be reproduced.






Note



Trend clustering is exploratory. Membership in a K-means cluster does not establish statistical significance for every protein in that cluster. Use DEP or an appropriate time-series/repeated-measures model when formal statistical inference is required.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Use Multi-omics → Co-enrichment after enrichment analysis has been completed separately for multiple omics layers, contrasts, tissues, or protein clusters. The module compares enrichment results across two or three omics datasets, identifies shared and omics-specific pathways, and provides publication-oriented summary tables and plots.
The most important requirement is comparability: enrichment results should use compatible pathway identifiers, annotation versions, and biological backgrounds. A pathway appearing in only one layer can reflect true biology, but it can also arise from incompatible annotation systems or different background universes.

text:
Co-enrichment interface
The screenshot below shows the current three-omics example with Transcriptome, Proteome, and Metabolome enrichment results. The interface contains Data Input, Column Mapping, Display Control, Color & Export, and Run & Download controls. The result area provides an overlap summary, source-data previews, a summary bar plot, a matrix-style UpSet plot, a significance bubble plot, and a table of shared/specific pathways.






Figure 1: ProtVis Co-enrichment interface showing a three-omics example with Transcriptome, Proteome and Metabolome enrichment results, overlap summary, UpSet-style overlap visualization and pathway significance outputs.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Recommended operating order
1. Choose two-omics or three-omics mode. Open Data Input and select Co-enrichment Mode. Use Two-omics when comparing two result sets and Three-omics when comparing three layers such as transcriptome, proteome and metabolome.
2. Name each omics layer. Set Omics 1 Name, Omics 2 Name, and, in three-omics mode, Omics 3 Name. These labels are propagated into summaries and plots, so use concise names that match the biological analysis.
3. Load enrichment results. Upload the enrichment file for each omics layer. ProtVis accepts .csv, .tsv, .txt, .xlsx, and .xls. For a quick demonstration, click Use built-in example data. The built-in example loads representative Transcriptome, Proteome and Metabolome enrichment tables; review the mappings and then run the analysis.
4. Set the adjusted p-value cutoff. The default Adjusted p-value cutoff is 0.05. Pathways are considered significant in each layer according to this threshold before shared/specific classifications are summarized.
5. Decide how duplicate pathway names are handled. Keep Remove duplicated pathway names within each omics selected unless there is a specific reason to preserve duplicate descriptions. This avoids counting the same pathway more than once inside one omics layer.
6. Verify Column Mapping. Open Column Mapping and, for each uploaded dataset, select the correct Pathway column and Adjusted p-value column. ProtVis attempts to guess these fields, but the selections should still be checked manually before running the comparison.
7. Configure Display Control. Choose Pathway Display Mode as All, Shared only, or Specific only. Use the group filter to focus on one overlap class when needed. Top N pathways in bubble plot controls how many pathways are shown in the bubble visualization; the current default is 20. The value-label and sorting options affect presentation rather than pathway classification.
8. Configure colors and export settings. Under Color & Export, customize colors for shared pathways, pairwise-shared pathways, and omics-specific groups. The UpSet active/inactive colors and bubble low/high colors can also be adjusted. Choose PDF or PNG for plot downloads; PNG export additionally uses the selected DPI.
9. Run the analysis. Open Run & Download and click Run. After processing, review the summary note above the overlap table to confirm the adjusted p-value cutoff, display mode, group filter, and Top N setting used for the current result.
10. Inspect the result panels. Overlap Summary reports the pathway classes and counts. Uploaded Data Preview lets you inspect the input enrichment tables. Summary Bar Plot compares class sizes, Matrix-style UpSet Plot shows overlap structure, Significance Bubble Plot summarizes pathway significance across layers, and Shared and Specific Pathways provides the underlying pathway-level table.
11. Export tables and plots. The Run & Download section provides downloadable two-omics and three-omics demo data, the summary table, the pathway table, and individual summary, UpSet, and bubble plots in the selected format.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Recommended input structure
Each omics enrichment file must contain at least a pathway/term field and an adjusted p-value field. Additional columns can be retained. A minimal example is:
Pathway,padj,Count
Carbon metabolism,0.003,28
Ribosome,0.018,35
Plant hormone signal transduction,0.021,19
Column names do not have to match this example exactly because they are assigned explicitly in Column Mapping.

title: Co-enrichment
section: How shared and specific pathways should be interpreted
text:
How shared and specific pathways should be interpreted
A pathway classified as shared is present among the significant enrichment results of more than one selected omics layer. A pathway classified as specific is significant only in the corresponding layer under the current cutoff. In three-omics mode, ProtVis can distinguish pathways shared by all three layers, pairwise-shared pathways, and pathways specific to one layer.
Do not interpret overlap alone as evidence that molecular changes occur in the same direction or involve the same genes/proteins/metabolites. Co-enrichment compares pathway-level enrichment membership; directionality and constituent features should be checked in the original differential and enrichment results.

title: Co-enrichment
text:
Practical checks before interpretation
Confirm that all input tables use the same pathway naming/ID system, that enrichment backgrounds are biologically comparable, and that the adjusted p-values were calculated in a compatible way. If pathway descriptions differ only because of database-version naming changes, harmonize identifiers before upload.






Tip



For cross-omics comparisons, stable pathway identifiers are preferable to free-text descriptions whenever they are available. Descriptions can change between database releases even when the underlying pathway is the same.








Note



The pathways and counts shown in the screenshot belong to the built-in demonstration and are intended to illustrate the interface. Real results depend on the uploaded enrichment tables, column mappings, p-value cutoff, and display filters.

title: PTM analysis
text:
The PTM section is intended for modification-centric proteomics workflows in which peptide/site-level evidence needs to be inspected separately from ordinary protein abundance analysis.
Because PTM search-engine exports differ substantially in site localization, peptide sequence, modification notation and protein mapping, always check that the selected source parser and input columns match the dataset that generated the evidence.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Recommended workflow

Complete the standard project setup and source selection.
Open PTM and load the PTM-specific table expected by the module.
Verify modified sequence/site notation and protein identifiers before filtering.
Apply localization/evidence filters appropriate to the experiment.
Inspect modification-level quantitative patterns separately from total protein abundance.
Export the filtered evidence table used for every figure.

title: PTM analysis
text:
Biological interpretation
A change at a phosphosite, acetylation site or other PTM can reflect altered modification occupancy, altered total protein abundance, or both. When possible, compare PTM abundance with the corresponding protein-level signal before assigning a regulatory interpretation.






Warning



Do not interpret a modified peptide as a unique site when the search result does not localize the modification confidently. Preserve the original localization evidence in the exported record.

title: Project init
text:
Project init establishes the analysis context shared by all later modules. It defines the writable project directory, sample metadata, data source, and—when already available—the quantitative expression matrix. It then creates the first validated ProtVis_dataset and saves the initial project stage.
The current interface supports two distinct starting patterns:

Tabular quantitative data: sample metadata + an expression matrix or a built-in source example.
Raw/mzML + Sage: sample metadata + mzML directory + protein FASTA. In this route, Project init can create a valid Sage staging object before an expression matrix exists.

Common inputs

Supported source selections

title: Project init
text:
Raw/mzML + Sage workflow
Choose this route when the starting material is converted mass-spectrometry data in mzML format and you want ProtVis to run the Sage database search. The full-resolution screenshot below is the original PNG uploaded from the running application; the red labels show the required operating order.






Figure 1: Raw/mzML Project init workflow in ProtVis. The red labels indicate the recommended order: 1 set working directory, 2 upload sample information, 3 upload protein FASTA, 4 select the mzML input directory, 5 check mzML files, 6 select Raw as the data source, and 7 run Project init. The right panel shows the six PXD065315 control samples after successful initialization.




Follow the numbered order in the figure
1. Set the working directory. Click Set working directory and choose a local directory in which ProtVis can create stage files, portable exports, the Sage_search directory and later analysis outputs. The illustrated project uses E:/count/p_raw. The directory must exist and be writable. Keeping one analysis inside a stable project directory makes checkpoint and Sage-result recovery much more reliable.
2. Load the sample information. Upload a .csv, .xlsx, or .xls table with at least sample_id and mzml_file, or click Use built-in PXD065315 sample information for the six-sample maize control example. Wait for Upload complete, then inspect the Sample Info preview. For the built-in example, the six rows are B73_C1, B73_C2, B73_C3, EA2024_C1, EA2024_C2, and EA2024_C3; the mzml_file field must point to the corresponding .mzML names.
3. Upload the protein FASTA. Under Raw/mzML input, upload the protein database used for Sage. Accepted inputs include .fa, .fasta, .faa, and supported compressed FASTA forms. Use a FASTA that matches the organism and protein identifiers expected for the experiment. In the illustrated maize example, UP000007305_4577.fasta is registered. Do not continue until the interface reports FASTA ready.
4. Select the mzML input directory. Click Select mzML input directory and choose the folder containing the converted mzML files. The folder may also contain the original vendor .raw files, but the check is performed against the .mzML filenames registered in sample_info. For PXD065315, the expected converted files are B73_C1.mzML, B73_C2.mzML, B73_C3.mzML, EA2024_C1.mzML, EA2024_C2.mzML, and EA2024_C3.mzML.
5. Check the mzML files. Click Check mzML files. ProtVis verifies that filenames are unique, have the .mzML extension and exist in the selected directory. Resolve every Missing or Invalid extension row before initializing the project. If a check fails, compare the physical filename with sample_info$mzml_file character by character.
6. Select Raw as the data source. In Select data source, choose Raw. This activates the Raw/Sage route and exposes the top-level Search tab. Do not upload a fabricated expression matrix merely to satisfy Project init; the expression layer is deliberately absent until Sage produces LFQ results.
7. Run Project init. Click the large Project init button. A successful Raw initialization reports “PROJECT INIT completed — Sage ProtVis_dataset is ready.” Inspect the preview tabs after completion. Sample Info should contain the expected rows, Raw/mzML Files should reflect the registered files, and Expression Matrix can remain empty at this stage. The next step is Search, not Correct Noise.
When an uploaded sample table contains an mzML filename column (mzml_file, mzml, raw_file, file, or filename), ProtVis automatically registers it for the Sage workflow.






ImportantDo not create a fake expression matrix



A Raw/Sage project does not need a protein expression matrix before Search. Project init creates a Sage_staging project object and fills the expression layer only after LFQ results are available. After Step 7 succeeds, continue directly to Raw/mzML + Sage search.




The Sage staging object
If no expression matrix exists yet, Project init creates a staging ProtVis_dataset with sample metadata and registered input paths. Its workflow stage is Sage_staging, with an object name such as:
ProtVis_dataset__project_init__Sage_staging__v1
This is intentional. ProtVis does not fabricate protein abundances before the database search. The staging object is valid even though its expression layer is temporarily empty. Step1_project_init.rda and the portable export are still written, so the project has a recoverable starting state.

title: Project init
text:

title: Project init
text:
Common validation problems
Raw project creates no expression preview. This is expected before Sage Search. The staging object intentionally has no protein abundance matrix.
mzML check reports Missing. The mzml_file values must match the files in the selected directory. The check is case-aware at the filesystem level and also rejects non-mzML extensions or duplicate names.
Sample names do not match a tabular matrix. Check sample_id, maxquant_id, and expression-matrix column names. Do not silently reorder samples outside ProtVis without recording the change.
Working directory cannot be selected. Choose a local directory you can write to. ProtVis normalizes selected paths and rejects inaccessible locations instead of continuing with an invalid project directory.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Overview interface
The full-resolution screenshot below shows the current Overview/QC page using the six-sample maize example. Values such as 5,209 proteins and 6 samples belong to this example and should not be treated as fixed ProtVis output sizes.






Figure 1: ProtVis Overview and quality-control interface. The left panel begins with Load Data and provides Correlation, Expression pattern and Dimensionality Reduction controls. The main area compares dimensionality-reduction results before and after normalization and summarizes proteomics QC, missingness and sample-level intensity diagnostics.




Recommended operating order
1. Load the project data. Open Downstream analysis → Overview and click Load Data. ProtVis loads the imputed and normalized quantitative states needed for side-by-side diagnostics. Confirm the status message before interpreting any plot. In the screenshot, both datasets load successfully and each contains 5,209 proteins across 6 samples.
2. Inspect correlation first. Open Correlation, choose Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall, and inspect whether samples expected to be biologically similar cluster together. Correlation is especially useful for identifying a single failed replicate or a sample whose overall profile is inconsistent with its group.
3. Inspect the expression-pattern heatmap. Use Expression pattern to view broad abundance structure among the most variable proteins. This view is intended for global pattern checking rather than formal differential-abundance inference. If scaling is enabled, interpret relative patterns rather than absolute abundance differences.
4. Compare dimensionality reduction before and after normalization. In Dimensionality Reduction, choose PCA, PCoA, t-SNE, UMAP, or NMDS. The screenshot uses UMAP and displays results before normalization and after normalization side by side. A useful normalization should reduce unwanted technical structure without erasing biologically plausible separation.
5. Set grouping aesthetics from sample metadata. Color and 95% confidence ellipses can use metadata such as group, tissue, species, batch, or condition; point shape can be assigned independently. In the illustrated interface, tissue is used for color/ellipse grouping and species for point shape. Use fields that match the actual experimental design rather than forcing the demo defaults onto another dataset.
6. Finish with the proteomics QC panel. Review the Proteomics QC summary, missing-value rate by sample, sample total normalized intensity, intensity distributions, PCA/CV diagnostics and related summaries. Unexpectedly high missingness, a large sample-level intensity shift, or a single isolated sample should be investigated before DEP analysis.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Correlation
Choose Pearson, Spearman, or Kendall correlation, then configure clustering and whether correlation values/sample names are displayed. Replicates do not need to be identical, but samples from the same biological condition should usually be more similar to one another than to unrelated groups unless the experiment provides a biological reason otherwise.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Expression pattern
The expression-pattern heatmap can focus on the top variable features and optionally scale by protein or sample. This is useful for identifying broad coordinated patterns, outlier samples and dominant abundance blocks. It should not replace a statistical DEP model.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Dimensionality reduction
Available methods are:

PCA
PCoA
t-SNE
UMAP
NMDS

ProtVis displays dimensionality reduction before normalization and after normalization so that the effect of preprocessing can be assessed directly. For stochastic methods such as t-SNE or UMAP, interpret neighborhood structure together with the experimental design rather than treating axis values as directly comparable biological quantities.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Proteomics QC
The QC panel summarizes and exports key diagnostics including sample total intensity, sample missing-value rate, intensity boxplots/density, PCA based on variable features, coefficient-of-variation distributions and the normalized matrix.






WarningDo not select a preprocessing strategy only because a plot looks cleaner



A visually tighter PCA or UMAP is not proof that preprocessing is correct. If normalization creates separation that conflicts with known biology, removes a strong expected effect, or produces implausible sample distributions, return to the preceding preprocessing stages and check the assumptions.

title: Overview & QC
text:
Handoff to DEP analysis
Once sample relationships, missingness, distributions and group structure are acceptable, continue to DEP analysis. Keep the Overview/QC outputs as part of the analysis record because they provide the context needed to judge the reliability of downstream differential results.
